extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political science; informed general readers interested in party systems and public administration
extracted.subtask_description: Expository chapter-level analysis of political 'rings' and the Spoils System: when and why political machines arise, how patronage and rotation in office operate, their effects on administration, and the early civil-service reforms (Pendleton Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood of rings by city size
rubrics_metrics.description: Rings are much less likely to exist in the smaller cities, though a population of 30,000 or 40,000 may occasionally support them. We should hardly find them in a city below 10,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Original text gives numeric thresholds and regional reports: Missouri said 'few or no rings in cities under 60,000 inhabitants'; Kentucky noted exceptions (Lexington at 22,000; Frankfort with less). Use city population and presence of a 'floating irresponsible following' as predictors of ring existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban conditions favoring rings and bosses
rubrics_metrics.description: Large cities with concentrated immigrant populations and a floating, irresponsible following are favourable to the growth of rings and bosses; local business interests (e.g., liquor-saloon keepers) may combine to 'run politics'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Detroit, New York, Philadelphia, Buffalo, and New Orleans. The text attributes prevalence to scale, concentrated immigrant masses, and commercial interests that seek friendly municipal management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rural and small-town resistance to rings
rubrics_metrics.description: Country places and smaller cities are generally not ring-ridden: immigrants are scattered among natives, settlers (Germans, Scandinavians) assimilate, and the country voter is less exposed to temptations and less easy to lead or drive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Boss has 'no occupation' in such places; where cliques exist they are often local lawyers combining to hold offices in turn and do little harm. Exceptions arise under special circumstances (e.g., unusual local wealth or absentee taxpayers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essential features of the Spoils System
rubrics_metrics.description: The essential features are that a place in the public service is held at the absolute pleasure of the appointing authority; it is invariably bestowed from party motives on a party man as a reward for party services; no man expects to hold it any longer than his party holds power; and this gives him the strongest personal reasons for fighting in the party ranks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This passage is given nearly verbatim in the text as the definition of the system's mechanics; use these four features to identify spoils-style patronage in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular rationales for rotation in office
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotation in office was (and is by many) held to be conformable to the genius of a democracy: it gives every man an equal chance, stimulates exertion, prevents the growth of an official caste, and recognizes equality by making officials servants not masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter explains civic beliefs (e.g., comparison to Athenian/Florentine lot systems, American fondness for novelty) that justified rotation; these rationales help explain why patronage persisted despite its harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of the Spoils System on politics and administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The system produced a class of professional politicians and bosses, degraded public morals, turned politics into the art of distributing salaries to secure support, distracted leaders from national problems, and fostered election frauds (repeating, ballot stuffing, obstruction, fraudulent counting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text documents concrete administrative and ethical harms: lower administrative competence, insincerity, cynicism, and organization of party machines that manipulate primaries and conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage via local recommendation and senatorial influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidents and ministers, lacking local knowledge of distant applicants, naturally relied on senators or representatives from the State or district to recommend candidates, which encouraged the admission of political claims to appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains causal mechanism: need for local information + Senate confirmation incentives produced reliance on local political leaders and thus strengthened patronage networks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation undermines civil service competence and incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Insecure tenure discourages sedulous application to work; the civil service is not a career under rotation, and administration lags behind private enterprises; officials focus on party duties rather than public service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links insecure tenure to lack of skill accumulation and to officials' duty to patrons rather than the public, producing poorer performance especially in higher grades (departments at Washington, major custom-houses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Civil service reform and the Pendleton Act (classified service)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pendleton Act (1883) instituted a board of civil-service commissioners to apply competitive examinations to many departmental offices, creating a 'classified service' to which the examination system applied, and thereby reduced the percentage of political removals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance notes: Presidents (Arthur, Cleveland, Roosevelt) extended the Act's scope; classified service still experienced some political removals, but far fewer than the unclassified service. The chapter highlights competitive examination as the principal reform mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional/social composition differences affecting ring growth (the South)
rubrics_metrics.description: The South's social composition (scarcity of European immigrants; presence of negroes and 'poor whites'; stronger traditional local leadership) produced different patterns: bosses could potentially exploit ignorant voters, yet entrenched local elites often prevented serious ring mischief; exceptions include New Orleans, and certain Texas/Arkansas cities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use regional social structure, poverty, and persistence of social leadership as predictors; the chapter cites Galveston as an example where the commission form of government displaced a ring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bosses' method of maintaining power through patronage distribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Boss consolidates and extends power by bestowal of patronage, dividing the spoils before and after elections: promising higher elective offices to major supporters and dispensing minor appointive offices as rewards and stepping-stones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter uses metaphor ('giver of rings') and practical mechanics: minor offices bind rank-and-file by hope of advancement and fear of loss; patronage is both carrot and chain sustaining the Machine.
